newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ referendum on compulsory savings by Sept - Birch.
newsitem.headline: NZ referendum on compulsory savings by Sept - Birch.

text.p: New Zealand Finance Minister Bill Birch said on Wednesday a referendum on the new compulsory savings scheme, detailed in the coalition agreement, would be held no later than September.

If the scheme received public support it would be introduced by July 1, 1998, Birch said, confirming an undertaking in the December 1996 coalition agreement between the National and New Zealand First parties.
"The outcome of that one is firmly in the hands of the voting public," Birch said in a speech to the Institute for International Research's annual tax conference.
Birch said if the compulsory savings scheme proceeded, it quite clearly had major tax implications.

An initial contribution rate of three percent in 1998-99 would rise to eight percent by 2002, he said, again quoting from the coalition agreement. Birch said this would be offset, assuming adequate surpluses, by additional tax cuts during that period.
The coalition would also abolish from April 1 next year the superannuation surcharge on pensioners' income, which Birch said had been contentious ever since Labour introduced it.

Birch said the New Zealand tax system was regarded internationally as one of the least distorted in the world. The National/New Zealand First coalition would maintain both the impetus and direction of the tax reform process since 1990.

"We remain fully committed to a broad-base low-rate approach, designed to minimise the distortionary impact of tax on investment, production, employment and training decisions, whether by firms or individuals," Birch said.
He said looking ahead into the next three years, the new government had a "very substantial" range of tax issues on the table.
Tax on conduit incomes was impacting adversely on overseas investors in foreign companies operating in New Zealand, a category into which most of the major New Zealand corporates fell.
"At present, we discourage foreign investors from using those companies as investment vehicles in overseas countries. That's not a lot of benefit to New Zealand."
Birch said the centre-right coalition government agreed that progress in the area of tax simplification was "urgently desirable".

Taxation of life and superannuation fund savings was another issue. The report by a joint public and private sector working party looking into the current system, originally scheduled for December, was now expected in mid to late March.
Reports were also being prepared on trans-Tasman investment and tax issues.

Birch said the 1997 government budget was clearly the coalition government's overwhelming priority at present, but by the end of March the government should be well on the way to indicating the shape of a new tax policy work programme.
